items.followUp: State the main limitation of Dobereiner’s classification of elements.

rubric.why: Identifies the number of elements and their shared chemical properties.
rubric.description: A triad consists of three elements with similar properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both that there are three elements and that their properties are similar.

rubric.why: Gives the defining relationship between the atomic masses of the three elements.
rubric.description: The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the other two.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the approximate mean relationship.

modelAnswer: Dobereiner’s Triads are groups of three elements with similar chemical properties.
In each triad, the atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two elements.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds usually have high melting points?

rubric.why: Identifies the strong force holding the ions together.
rubric.description: Oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the strong electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions.

rubric.why: Links the strong attractions to the solid structure of an ionic compound.
rubric.description: The ions are held in fixed positions in a crystal lattice, making the compound solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ions are fixed in a lattice or otherwise explaining that the structure is solid.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
The ions are held in fixed positions in a crystal lattice, so ionic compounds are solids.

items.followUp: How do atoms form ions when they react?

rubric.why: States the stability atoms achieve through reacting.
rubric.description: Atoms react to attain a stable electronic configuration, usually like that of a noble gas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the stable configuration or complete outer shell.

rubric.why: Describes how atoms achieve the stable configuration.
rubric.description: Atoms lose, gain, or share valence electrons to attain a stable configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are transferred or shared.

modelAnswer: Atoms react with one another to attain a stable electronic configuration, usually like that of a noble gas.
They do this by losing, gaining, or sharing valence electrons.

items.followUp: Why do solid ionic compounds not conduct electricity, while their solutions do?

rubric.why: Identifies that ions can move in molten or dissolved ionic compounds.
rubric.description: In molten form or solution, the ions are free to move.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the ions become mobile or free to move.

rubric.why: Explains how mobile ions allow electric current to pass.
rubric.description: The moving ions carry electric charge through the molten compound or solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the movement of ions to carrying charge or conducting electricity.

modelAnswer: In solution or molten form, the ions in an ionic compound are free to move.
These mobile ions carry electric charge, so the solution or molten compound conducts electricity.

items.followUp: What kinds of solutes dissolve best in polar and non-polar solvents?

rubric.why: States the matching rule for polar substances.
rubric.description: Polar solutes generally dissolve in polar solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the polar-in-polar part of the principle.

rubric.why: States the matching rule for non-polar substances.
rubric.description: Non-polar solutes generally dissolve in non-polar solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the non-polar-in-non-polar part of the principle.

modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that polar solutes generally dissolve in polar solvents.
Similarly, non-polar solutes generally dissolve in non-polar solvents.

rubric.why: Defines saturation by the limit on the amount of solute dissolved.
rubric.description: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a particular temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that no more solute can dissolve, or that the maximum amount has dissolved.

rubric.why: Recognises that solubility depends on temperature.
rubric.description: The maximum amount is specified for a particular temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying that the definition applies at a particular temperature.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution is one that contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
Any additional solute remains undissolved at that temperature.

items.followUp: Name four highly reactive metals from the reactivity series.

rubric.why: Credits two correct examples from the moderately reactive metals.
rubric.description: Any two suitable examples, such as zinc, iron, tin, and lead.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming any two different moderately reactive metals.

rubric.why: Credits the remaining correct examples to make a set of four.
rubric.description: Four suitable examples are zinc, iron, tin, and lead.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least four different moderately reactive metals.

modelAnswer: Four moderately reactive metals are zinc (Zn), iron (Fe), tin (Sn), and lead (Pb).

rubric.why: Identifies the outer-shell electron arrangement responsible for alkali-metal reactivity.
rubric.description: An alkali metal has one electron in its outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that alkali metals have one valence electron.

rubric.why: Explains that the single outer electron is readily lost, producing a stable ion.
rubric.description: Alkali metals readily lose this electron to form stable +1 ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the easy loss of the outer electron to formation of a stable positive ion.

modelAnswer: Alkali metals have one electron in their outermost shell.
They readily lose this electron to form stable +1 ions, which makes them extremely reactive.
